## Answer

**No.** Lebesgue measurability of a function $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb{C}$ does **not** imply that $f$ is Lebesgue integrable. A measurable function is integrable if and only if $\int_{[a,b]}|f|\,d\mu<\infty$, and measurability alone does not guarantee this.

### Counterexample

Take $[a,b]=[0,1]$ and define
$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{1}{x}, & x\in(0,1],\\[4pt] 0, & x=0.\end{cases}$$

**Measurability.** On $(0,1]$ the function $f$ coincides with $x\mapsto 1/x$, which is continuous (hence Borel measurable) on $(0,1]$. The singleton $\{0\}$ is a Borel set, and modifying a measurable function on a null set preserves measurability. Therefore $f$ is Lebesgue measurable on $[0,1]$.

**Non-integrability.** For every $n\ge 1$,
$$\int_{[1/n,\,1]}|f|\,d\mu=\int_{1/n}^{1}\frac{dx}{x}=\ln n.$$
Since $|f|\ge 0$ is measurable, by the monotone convergence theorem (applied to $|f|\cdot\mathbf{1}_{[1/n,1]}$ as $n\to\infty$),
$$\int_{[0,1]}|f|\,d\mu=\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_{1/n}^{1}\frac{dx}{x}=\lim_{n\to\infty}\ln n=+\infty.$$
Thus $f\notin L^{1}([0,1])$.

### Conclusion

Lebesgue integrability of a complex-valued function on $[a,b]$ requires both measurability **and** finiteness of $\int_{[a,b]}|f|\,d\mu$. The example above is measurable yet has infinite $L^{1}$-norm, so measurability alone is strictly weaker than integrability.

### PROOF COMPLETE
